v: A brutal oppression drama wrapped in proper commercial packaging — and for audiences like me, that packaging is exactly what makes it click 😄
e: DC takes a familiar oppression-and-police-brutality setup and packages it as a surprisingly effective commercial entertainer. The performances, cinematography and especially the classical-music-infused BGM made the violence land far better for me than I expected.
body:
I generally stay away from the overcooked Tamil-flavoured oppression & brutality stories... but couldn’t control myself with all the FOMO created by the feedback from those who watched it. So much so that I had to ditch Srinu, my regular Partner in Crime for watching such movies!!!! 😜

And do I have any regret or guilt about ditching him? Absolutely not 😉 But can’t deny the fact that I would have enjoyed it even more in his company!!! Don’t worry Srinu, we will compensate with Toxicity 😉😂

Coming back to the movie... unlike the epics of Kabali or Kaala, DC is a proper oppression and fight-against-police-brutality movie, but packed into a proper commercial entertainer that somehow still feels realistic. And that’s largely because of the extraordinary effort from all the actors, cinematographer and music director 🙏

Special mention to the BGM 🤯 I feel Animal started the trend of using old songs to elevate the audience experience of a scene, which Dhurandhar bettered by using vintage & contrasting songs as BGM for violent scenes. But DC took it one step further by using classical music to elevate the emotions during violence 🫡 What a combination!!!

Initially, I was surprised to hear that this movie wasn’t doing that well with the Tamil audience but clicked really well with the Telugu audience. After watching it, I understood why.

Tamil movie lovers still cherish those raw, grounded and realistic oppression movies, whereas this one is packaged commercially. That may not have worked as much for them... but for audiences like me, that commercial packaging is exactly what made it click 😄

v: A visual spectacle with terrific performances, but for me it remains exactly this: Too Much Quality with No Clarity.
e: The scale, locations, CGI and performances are unquestionably richer this time, but the magic that made Kantara work for me is missing. I kept seeing a commercially upgraded spectacle when I was hoping for a deeper dive into the folklore and origins behind the legend.
body:
DISCLAIMER: Don’t worry, I’m not on some secret mission to hate or hype this movie. This is just what I honestly felt after watching it — NO FAN CLUB, NO HATE CLUB. Just me and my opinion.

When I first watched Kantara, I didn’t have any expectations and I was completely blown away by the approach of blending folklore, terrific visuals and acting into a very simple and common story of a land dispute.

Coming to Kantara: Chapter 1, obviously I had expectations from the previous movie...

On the positive side... this time the budget has been hiked, and you can see the grandeur on the big screen with the story being set in a king’s era. The locations looked more realistic than in the previous part. The CGI work was more polished, the cast had more familiar faces this time, and everyone did an excellent job.

For Kantara, I remember how I was going bonkers about how Rishab Shetty had written, directed and acted in the movie... This time too, he did it all by himself. Unfortunately, what worked for me in Kantara didn’t work for me in Kantara: Chapter 1.

My eyes were in for a treat with the visual spectacle on screen, but somehow it wasn’t creating the much-needed impact on my other senses 😪 All I could think of was a commercially upgraded version made to cash in on the craze of Kantara.

The BGM again felt like a rehashed version of Kantara and failed to create much impact for me this time. Acting-wise, Rishab Shetty was good as usual, but this time I always knew how his hand and leg movements would be and how his facial expressions would change whenever he was possessed. It felt like I was watching the same Kantara performance again, so the Vaaaaaaaaav feeling was missing this time.

Special shout-out to Gulshan Devaiah, who was excellent as King Kulashekara and was the only reason I didn’t think of walking out of this film with disappointment 🫡

Also, if not for the individual performances by Rukmini and Jayaram, there was hardly any scope in the story — except in the climax — to elevate their characters, because the movie was only and only focused on elevating Rishab.

When the film itself is named Chapter 1, I was expecting Rishab Shetty to dive deep into his region’s folklore and give us the origin story of Panjurli, Guliga, Bhoota Kola and finally how Kantara was formed... but instead, he focused on exploring the story of tribal leader Berme, played by Rishab himself.

While Kantara’s execution revolved around the land dispute and how Guliga protects Panjurli’s land and promise, with Rishab Shetty’s character moulding itself perfectly into the story flow, Chapter 1 is all about the commercial rise, fall and rise of Berme — with the actual story going for a toss!!!!

On a final note... Kantara: Chapter 1 is Too Much Quality with No Clarity.

v: Average gangster content on paper, but Sujeeth + Thaman turn it into a proper PK fan trance — and the forgotten fan in me was fully satisfied!
e: The story is below average and neutral viewers may not get the same high, but Sujeeth knows exactly what kind of film he is making. A handful of adrenaline-pumping PK moments, powered by Thaman’s terrific BGM, are enough to turn OG into a proper fan celebration.
body:
It’s truly a Pawan Kalyan film — made for the fans, by the fans, and dedicated to the fans!

The bigger the fan, the stronger the trance this movie creates. Fans will definitely watch it multiple times just to relive the high.

For neutral audiences, the movie might feel like average commercial content, similar to films like Jailer, Leo, Pathaan or Good Bad Ugly.

Content-wise, it follows the regular commercial gangster format, with stylish scenes and terrific background music from Thaman 🙏 The story itself is below average and can test your patience. The much-hyped Saaho connection also didn’t fit in well for me.

Still, I admire Sujeeth’s effort. He had to work with very limited dates from Pawan, who has always relied more on his screen charisma than acting range. Within those limits, Sujeeth managed to create 4–5 adrenaline-pumping scenes that drove fans crazy and made them forget the flaws.

Thaman’s music elevated the film into a treat for fans. He is the real HERO of this movie — I can’t even dare to imagine this film without his BGM 🙏🙏

Neutral viewers may not enjoy it as much as fans. My real frustration, however, is with self-proclaimed reviewers who criticise every movie without understanding its intent. This film was always promoted as a cult fan movie, not a national-award-level story. Expecting otherwise is just unfair and shows just how big an IDIOT you are.

Though I usually watch films as a neutral movie lover, Sujeeth succeeded in waking up the long-forgotten PK fan in me — and satisfied him to the core!

v: A VERY GOOD mythological superhero entertainer with spectacular CGI — but as a film buff, I can’t stop seeing the EPIC franchise opportunity that was missed 😢
e: MIRAI gets a lot right with its mythology-meets-commercial-cinema idea, impressive CGI, production values and committed performances. But the hero, villain and Ashoka’s hidden-books mythology deserved far more depth; what could have been an epic multipart franchise feels rushed into one film.
body:
Let me make this clear: this is not a Cult Classic Movie, but it is a VERY GOOD movie with a proper mix of fiction & mythology along with commercial elements!!! A good movie about how an underdog turns into a superhero with a touch of the Puranas!!!

Wait a minute... why do I have a déjà vu of reviewing Hanu-Man!! Teja Sajja should have done at least a movie or two before committing to MIRAI, just to give the audience a fair chance to enjoy this movie without constantly comparing it with Hanu-Man!!!

Content-wise, the film had a lot to explore in the villain’s arc, the hero’s arc and their final clash — enough potential to become a multipart movie with a grand climax. But somewhere, I felt the director rushed into making the entire story a single-part movie.

When normal commercial movies like Devara and Kingdom have forcefully dragged their stories to make them two-part films, I am totally disappointed in Karthik, who is the writer and director here, for not putting a little more effort into the depth of the content. There was so much scope to make the story more informative about Ashoka’s nine hidden books and their contents, and to establish both the villain and hero’s character arcs properly. Instead, the film rushes to finish everything in a single part, leaving a few loose ends and a sense of dissatisfaction.

The execution of the CGI is the saving grace of this movie, along with top-notch production values. There are a few scenes that genuinely give you the vibe of watching a high-budget movie, and the team deserves special appreciation for that.

The BGM was very good and highlights the CGI-heavy scenes to give goosebumps for sure.

Acting-wise, Teja Sajja was perfect as an underdog-turned-superhero, but as I mentioned, he already played a similar character in Hanu-Man — the main difference being a village boy there versus a street-smart city boy here.

Manchu Manoj was perfect for this role and did complete justice to it. I only feel bad for him because the story writers didn’t put in that extra effort to dive deeper into his character. With stronger character-building, this could have become one of the most memorable villain roles in Indian movies — something on the level of Thanos.

Shriya Saran as Ambika was refreshing casting and she did complete justice to her role. Except for the Hindi Drishyam films, where she played a more conventional housewife character, I don’t think she has had many author-backed roles to properly showcase her acting skills — and man, she impressed me a lot here 😍

On a final note... this movie had everything in it to become an EPIC Multipart Franchise, potentially even bigger in scope than Baahubali or KGF, only to be let down by some lazy effort in the story-writing and screenplay departments 😡

As a normal audience member, you may either like this movie to the core or simply feel it is a good one-time watch. But as a film buff, I could easily see a Golden Opportunity Missed 😢
